title: Bhrigu Asks His Father
hook: a son asks his father to teach him Brahman, and the father only points: go find where everything comes from
carry: brahman: where everything comes from, lives in, returns to
tomorrow: salt disappears in a cup of water. where did it go?

segments.voice: Yesterday, Vedanta began with Shvetaketu: after the doing comes the wish to know Brahman.
screen: `THE WISH TO KNOW.` · `THEN WHAT IS BRAHMAN?`

segments.voice: In the Taittiriya Upanishad, a young man named Bhrigu goes to his father, the god Varuna, and asks straight out: sir, teach me Brahman. And his father won't hand him an answer. He gives him a few things to look at, food, breath, sight, hearing, mind, speech, and then one pointer. That from which these beings are born, by which they live, and into which they go when they leave: seek to know that. That is Brahman. Then he sends his son off to find it himself.
screen: `TEACH ME BRAHMAN.` → `NO ANSWER, ONE POINTER.` → `GO FIND IT.`

segments.voice: So Bhrigu sits with it, in tapas, deep, disciplined attention. He comes back: Brahman is food. Everything is born from food and lives on it. His father doesn't argue. He just says: seek it again, through tapas. Keep looking. Bhrigu goes deeper. Brahman is breath. Keep looking. Brahman is mind. Keep looking. Brahman is understanding. Keep looking. And the last time, Bhrigu understands: Brahman is bliss, ananda. From bliss these beings are born, by bliss they live, into bliss they return. That's the big teaching. Brahman isn't someone up in the sky, apart from the world, and it isn't one thing in the world. It's what the whole world comes from, rests in, and goes back to. The Brahma Sutra's second line says almost exactly Varuna's words: Brahman is that from which the birth and so on of this world come. Even schools that worship Brahman as a loving, personal God, like Ramanuja's, say the whole world lives within him. Vedanta teachers explain it with a picture: a parent shows a child the thin new moon by pointing at a branch just below it. The branch isn't the moon. It gets the eyes there. The Upanishad gives another line too, Brahman is truth, knowledge, the infinite, and some readers, Shankara among them, hear even that as pointing. And notice how Bhrigu learned. Each answer was true, and not the last word. Many teachers read his climb, food, breath, mind, understanding, bliss, as a path inward any seeker can walk.
screen: `FOOD. BREATH. MIND. UNDERSTANDING.` · `BLISS: ANANDA.` · `NOT A THING: THE SOURCE OF THINGS.` · `A BRANCH POINTING AT THE MOON.`

segments.voice: Climb Bhrigu's steps slowly. Feel your body, fed by food. Then your breath, coming and going. Then your mind, busy or quiet. Then the knowing that notices all of it. Then rest past the knowing, in whatever peace is there, without naming it. If you pray, you can let that peace be your prayer to the One you love.
Vedanta. Today, how it points to Brahman: that from which the world is born, by which it lives, into which it returns, and, Bhrigu found, bliss. Today's word.
Your line: Brahman, where everything comes from, lives in, and returns to. Not a thing, the source of things. See you tomorrow.

screen: `DAY 1193 COUNTS.` → `BRAHMAN: WHERE EVERYTHING COMES FROM, LIVES IN, RETURNS TO.` → `TOMORROW: WHERE DID THE SALT GO?`

howItsDone: In traditional Vedanta study, teachers explain the Brahma Sutra's second line alongside Taittiriya Upanishad 3.1 and 2.1, and the Bhriguvalli, Bhrigu's climb from food to bliss, is chanted and taught as part of the Taittiriya.

Brahman.meaning: the one reality everything comes from and returns to

Bhrigu.meaning: the son who asked his father to teach him Brahman

Varuna.meaning: Bhrigu's father, a god, who points but won't just tell

tapas.meaning: disciplined, deep effort; here, focused attention

ananda.meaning: bliss: Bhrigu's last answer for Brahman

Brahma Sutra 1.1.2 (that from which the origin and so on of this world come)
Taittiriya Upanishad 2.1 (Brahman is truth, knowledge, the infinite)
